title: Command of Evidence: Quantitative
kicker: American Diploma · Digital SAT · Reading and Writing · Information and Ideas
summary: Use tables, bar graphs and line graphs to back up a claim: read the data fast, match the claim and not just the numbers, and avoid the true-but-irrelevant trap — with four worked examples and a 10-question quiz.

blocks.text: What this question type tests

Some Reading and Writing passages on the Digital SAT come with a table, a bar graph or a line graph. Command of Evidence: Quantitative questions ask you to use the numbers to back up a statement in the text. The stem usually sounds like this (in our words): "Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?" or "Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to illustrate the researcher's claim?"

It is part of the **Information and Ideas** domain, together with Central Ideas and Details, Command of Evidence — Textual, and Inferences. These four skills together make up about 26% of the scored Reading and Writing questions (12–14 questions across both modules). Like every Reading and Writing question, it has one short passage (25–150 words) and four choices; here the passage simply includes some data as well.

This is **not a math question**. You only need to read values, compare them, and see a trend (going up, going down, bigger, smaller). The difficulty is logical: often **three or even all four choices state numbers that are true**. Only one of them proves the point the text is making.

blocks.title: أهم فكرة في السؤال ده
blocks.text: مش كفاية إن الأرقام اللي في الإجابة صح. أغلب الاختيارات بتكون أرقامها صح فعلاً من الجدول! الإجابة الصح هي اللي الأرقام بتاعتها بتثبت الجملة (الـ claim) اللي في القطعة. اقرأ الـ claim الأول، وبعدين دوّر في الجدول على الأرقام اللي تخدمها.
How to read a table or graph fast

items: **Read the title and labels first (5 seconds).** What is being measured? In what units (percent, thousands, minutes)? What are the rows/columns, or the x-axis and y-axis? Which line or bar is which group?
**Do NOT study every number.** You do not need all the data — only the part the claim talks about.
**Spot the big picture.** Going up or down? Which is highest and lowest? Do two lines move closer together or further apart?
**Now go to the text** and find the claim (often the sentence with the blank, or the sentence before it).

rows: Row and column headings; the units; the two cells the claim compares
"Group A was higher than Group B"; "X rose between two years"
Which bar is tallest/shortest; the label on each bar
"X was the most / least common"; "X was greater than Y"
Direction of each line; where lines cross; the gap between lines
"X increased steadily"; "the gap narrowed"; "X overtook Y"

blocks.text: **Note:** on this site, graphs inside practice questions are written as small text tables (for example, "Year | Visitors" with one row per year). Read them exactly as you would read the bars or points of a graph.
The method: match the claim, not just the numbers

items: **Find the claim and say it simply.** "The campaign worked best for plastic and paper." "Sleep falls every year of high school."
**Name what kind of claim it is.** A trend (rising/falling)? A comparison between groups? A highest/lowest? A gap that changes? Each type needs a different kind of data.
**Decide what the perfect data sentence must contain.** A trend needs at least a start and an end (and sometimes the middle). A comparison needs BOTH groups. "Both X and Y" needs both.
**Check every choice in two steps:** (1) Is it accurate according to the data? (2) Does it prove the claim? A choice must pass BOTH tests.
**Choose the one that passes both.** If two pass, pick the one that matches the claim more completely.

rows: Misread data (wrong row, wrong year, reversed)
Half of the claim (one group, one year)

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1 — Table, two-part claim**

In 2021, the town of Westfield ran a recycling campaign that focused only on paper and plastic. A council report on recycling rates (the percentage of each material that was recycled) concludes that the campaign worked: rates rose the most for the two materials that the campaign targeted.
**Question:** Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the report's conclusion?

items: A) Metal had the highest recycling rate of any material in 2020.
B) The recycling rate for plastic rose from 12% in 2020 to 25% in 2024.
C) Paper and plastic rates each rose by 13 percentage points between 2020 and 2024, while glass and metal rose by only 2 points each.
D) The recycling rate for paper rose from 48% in 2020 to 52% in 2024.

blocks.text: **Answer: C**

items: **A — ✗ Wrong.** True but irrelevant. Metal's 50% was indeed the highest in 2020, but the claim is about which materials rose the most.
**B — ✗ Wrong.** Half-right. True, and plastic was targeted, but the claim says the two targeted materials rose the MOST — you need both, and a comparison with the others.
**C — ✓ Correct.** Paper 48→61 and plastic 12→25 (both +13) against glass 35→37 and metal 50→52 (both +2). It shows the two targeted materials and the comparison with the untargeted ones.
**D — ✗ Wrong.** Misread. 52% is metal's 2024 rate; paper rose to 61%.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — Bar graph, a trend**
A health researcher surveyed students at several high schools about their sleep. She claims that the amount students sleep on school nights falls steadily as they move through high school.

headers: Average sleep on school nights (graph data)

blocks.text: **Question:** Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to illustrate the researcher's claim?

items: A) Average sleep went down every year, from 7.6 hours in grade 9 to 7.2, 6.8, and finally 6.5 hours in grade 12.
B) Students in grade 12 slept an average of 6.5 hours on school nights.
C) Students in grade 10 slept more on average than students in grade 11 did.
D) Students in grade 9 slept an average of less than 7 hours on school nights.

blocks.text: **Answer: A**

items: **A — ✓ Correct.** A trend claim ("falls steadily") needs the whole pattern. A gives every grade and shows a fall each year.
**B — ✗ Wrong.** Half-right. One value cannot show a trend; there is no comparison with earlier grades.
**C — ✗ Wrong.** True but too narrow. It compares only two grades, so it does not show a steady fall across all of high school.
**D — ✗ Wrong.** Misread. Grade 9 students slept 7.6 hours, which is more than 7.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — Line graph, two lines**

Bright lights near beaches can confuse nesting sea turtles. In 2018, Beach X introduced strict rules that limit lighting at night, while Beach Y introduced no rules. A conservation group argues that the data suggest the lighting rules may have helped turtles: ______
**Question:** Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the argument?

items: A) Beach Y had more turtle nests than Beach X did in 2018.
B) both beaches had more than 100 turtle nests in every year shown.
C) the number of nests at Beach X fell from 190 in 2018 to 120 in 2024.
D) the number of nests at Beach X rose from 120 in 2018 to 190 in 2024, while the number at Beach Y fell from 210 to 125.

blocks.text: **Answer: D**

items: **A — ✗ Wrong.** True but irrelevant. The starting numbers do not show any effect of the rules.
**B — ✗ Wrong.** True but irrelevant. It shows no difference between the beach with rules and the beach without them.
**C — ✗ Wrong.** Reversed. The Beach X line goes UP from 120 to 190, not down.
**D — ✓ Correct.** It shows nests rising where rules exist and falling where they do not — a comparison that points to the rules as the difference.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — Table, comparison between groups**

A science museum asked its visitors which type of exhibit they enjoyed most. The museum's director claims that visitors under 18 were much more interested in interactive science exhibits than older visitors were.
**Question:** Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the director's claim?

items: A) 31% of visitors aged 18 and older chose paintings as their favorite exhibit type.
B) 46% of visitors under 18 chose interactive science exhibits, compared with only 22% of visitors aged 18 and older.
C) Among visitors under 18, interactive science exhibits were chosen more often than any other exhibit type.
D) 22% of visitors under 18 chose interactive science exhibits.

blocks.text: **Answer: B**

items: **A — ✗ Wrong.** True but irrelevant. Paintings are not part of the claim.
**B — ✓ Correct.** The claim compares two age groups on one exhibit type. B gives the value for both groups and shows the big difference.
**C — ✗ Wrong.** Clever trap. It is true, but it compares exhibits WITHIN one age group. The claim compares the two age groups with each other.
**D — ✗ Wrong.** Misread: wrong column. 22% is the figure for visitors aged 18 and older.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **True but irrelevant:** the numbers are correct, but they are about a different group, year or item than the claim. This is the trap the test uses most.
**Half the claim:** one group when the claim compares two; one year when the claim is a trend; one material when the claim says "both".
**Wrong comparison:** comparing items inside one group when the claim compares two groups (Worked example 4, choice C).
**Misread data:** the wrong row or column, the wrong year, or numbers reversed ("fell from 190 to 120" instead of "rose from 120 to 190").
**Unit traps:** percent vs number, thousands vs units, percentage points vs percent.
**Outside information:** a choice that states something the data do not show (a cause, a future prediction, a group that is not in the table).

blocks.title: خطوتين لكل اختيار
blocks.text: اسأل نفسك سؤالين لكل اختيار: (١) الأرقام دي صح فعلاً من الجدول؟ (٢) الأرقام دي بتثبت الـ claim؟ لازم الإجابة تعدّي الاتنين. أغلب الإجابات الغلط بتعدّي السؤال الأول وتقع في التاني.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Read the sentence with the claim or the blank FIRST, then look at the data — you will know which numbers matter.
Glance at the title, units and labels; ignore the rest of the numbers until you need them.
Label the claim: trend, comparison, highest/lowest, or gap. Then ask what the data sentence must include.
Eliminate choices that mention a group, year or item the claim does not mention.
Check the remaining choice against the data, number by number, before you click. This takes 10 seconds and catches misreads.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Command of Evidence: Quantitative — Practice Quiz
blocks.intro: 10 questions in Digital SAT style. For each one: read the claim, label it (trend, comparison, highest/lowest, gap), then check that your choice is both accurate AND relevant.

questions.p:
Solar panels installed in Region K (thousands)
Year | Panels installed
2020 | 14
2021 | 19
2022 | 27
2023 | 38

An energy analyst notes that solar panel installations in Region K did not just rise every year from 2020 to 2023; the size of the yearly increase also grew. For example, ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
c: 38,000 panels were installed in Region K in 2023.
more panels were installed in 2021 than in 2020.
installations rose from 14,000 to 19,000, then to 27,000, and then to 38,000 — increases of 5,000, 8,000, and 11,000.
the number of panels installed doubled each year between 2020 and 2023.
questions.e: The claim has two parts: a rise every year AND bigger increases each year. Only C shows both. A and B are true but too narrow; D is inaccurate (14 to 19 is not doubling).

questions.p:
Average one-way commute in a city (minutes)
Transport | Minutes
Car | 38
Bus | 52
Metro | 31
Bicycle | 24

A student writing about city transport argues that, for workers in this city, the metro is a faster way to get to work than driving.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the student's argument?
c: The average metro commute was 31 minutes, compared with 38 minutes by car.
The bicycle had the shortest average commute, at 24 minutes.
The bus had the longest average commute of any type of transport.
The average metro commute was 38 minutes, compared with 31 minutes by car.
questions.e: The argument compares metro and car, so you need both values: 31 vs 38. B and C are true but about other kinds of transport; D reverses the numbers.

questions.p:
Average plant height after 4 weeks, by light color
Light color | Height (cm)
Red | 18.4
Blue | 15.1
Green | 9.7
White | 16.9

Because plant leaves reflect most green light instead of absorbing it, a team of botanists hypothesized that bean plants grown under green light would grow less than plants grown under any other color of light tested.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the botanists' hypothesis?
c: Plants grown under red light were the tallest, at an average of 18.4 cm.
Plants grown under white light grew taller on average than plants grown under blue light.
Plants grown under green light reached an average height of 15.1 cm.
Plants grown under green light averaged 9.7 cm, shorter than the plants under red, blue, or white light.
questions.e: The hypothesis is about green light being the lowest, so D (green vs all others) fits. A and B are true but do not mention green; C misreads the blue value.

questions.p:
Households with internet access in Country Z (%)
Year | Urban | Rural
2010 | 55 | 20
2015 | 70 | 38
2020 | 84 | 61
2025 | 91 | 79

A government report claims that the difference in internet access between urban and rural households in Country Z has become much smaller since 2010.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the report's claim?
c: Urban internet access rose from 55% of households in 2010 to 91% in 2025.
The gap between urban and rural access fell from 35 percentage points in 2010 to 12 percentage points in 2025.
Rural access was lower than urban access in every year shown.
Rural access in 2025 (79%) was higher than urban access in 2015 (70%).
questions.e: The claim is about the GAP, so you need both lines: 55−20 = 35 and 91−79 = 12. A uses only one line; C is true but does not show a change; D is a true but irrelevant cross-year comparison.

questions.p:
Preferred study time of 400 students (%)
Time of day | Students
Early morning | 18
Afternoon | 27
Evening | 41
Late night | 14

A school counselor wanted to show that relatively few students in the survey prefer to study at either end of the day. She noted that ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
c: the evening was the most popular study time, chosen by 41% of students.
only 18% of students chose early morning and only 14% chose late night.
early morning was chosen by 41% of the students surveyed.
more students chose the afternoon than chose the early morning.
questions.e: "Either end of the day" means early morning AND late night, so B gives both small figures. A and D are true but about other times; C misreads the evening figure.

questions.p:
Station | Elevation (m) | Yearly rainfall (mm)
Coastal | 10 | 640
Valley | 150 | 410
Foothill | 600 | 520
Mountain | 1,400 | 890

A geographer claims that, in this region, yearly rainfall always increases as elevation increases.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to weaken the geographer's claim?
c: The Mountain station, at the highest elevation, received the most rainfall: 890 mm.
The Foothill station received more rainfall than the Valley station did.
The Valley station received the least rainfall, 410 mm.
The Coastal station, at the lowest elevation (10 m), received more rainfall (640 mm) than both the Valley (150 m) and Foothill (600 m) stations.
questions.e: To weaken "always increases", you need a case where a lower station gets MORE rain than a higher one. D gives that case. A and B support the claim; C alone does not compare elevations.

questions.p:
City library loans by format (thousands)
Format | 2019 | 2024
Print books | 82 | 64
E-books | 21 | 47
Audiobooks | 6 | 19

A librarian reports that the way people borrow from the library has changed: between 2019 and 2024, digital loans grew while loans of print books fell. For instance, ______
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
c: e-book loans rose from 21,000 to 47,000 and audiobook loans from 6,000 to 19,000, while print loans dropped from 82,000 to 64,000.
print books were still the most borrowed format in 2024.
audiobook loans more than tripled between 2019 and 2024.
e-book loans fell from 47,000 in 2019 to 21,000 in 2024.
questions.e: The claim has two parts: digital up AND print down. A shows both. B is true but does not show change; C is true but covers only audiobooks; D reverses the years.

questions.p:
Average market price of tomatoes (local currency per kg)
Month | Price
January | 18
March | 15
May | 9
July | 7
September | 12
November | 20

A farmer explains that tomato prices at the market are lowest in the summer, when the harvest is largest, and much higher in the winter months.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to illustrate the farmer's explanation?
c: The price was highest in November, at 20 per kilogram.
The price in March was higher than the price in September.
The price fell to its lowest level, 7 per kilogram, in July, compared with 18 in January and 20 in November.
The price reached its lowest level, 7 per kilogram, in May.
questions.e: The explanation contrasts summer (lowest) and winter (much higher). C gives the July low and two winter values. A covers only winter; B is irrelevant; D misreads (May is 9).

questions.p:
Birds counted in two types of forest
Species | Old forest | Young plantation
Woodpeckers | 14 | 2
Owls | 6 | 1
Warblers | 22 | 19
Sparrows | 9 | 17

Woodpeckers and owls nest in holes in old or dead trees. An ecologist argues that these hole-nesting birds depend on old forests, where such trees are common.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the ecologist's argument?
c: Sparrows were more common in the young plantation than in the old forest.
Warblers were found in similar numbers in both types of forest.
More woodpeckers were counted in the young plantation than in the old forest.
The researchers counted 14 woodpeckers and 6 owls in the old forest but only 2 woodpeckers and 1 owl in the young plantation.
questions.e: The argument is about the hole-nesters (woodpeckers and owls) and the two forest types; D covers both birds in both forests. A and B are about other species; C reverses the data.

questions.p:
Participants who correctly recalled a word list (%)
Condition before the test | Participants
Full night's sleep | 78
Half night's sleep | 61
One-hour nap only | 59
No sleep | 44

In a memory study, researchers concluded that even a short nap helps memory compared with getting no sleep at all.
questions.q: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the researchers' conclusion?
c: 59% of participants who had a one-hour nap recalled the list correctly, compared with only 44% of those who had no sleep.
The highest recall rate, 78%, came after a full night's sleep.
Participants who slept half the night did slightly better than those who only had a nap.
59% of participants who had no sleep recalled the list correctly.
questions.e: The conclusion compares a nap with no sleep, so A gives both numbers. B and C are true but compare other conditions; D misreads the table.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Read the claim first, then only the part of the data it talks about.
Most wrong answers state TRUE numbers — they just do not prove the claim.
A trend needs a start and an end; a comparison needs both groups; "both X and Y" needs both.
Check every number in your choice against the data before you click: wrong row, wrong year and reversed values are common.
It is a reading question, not a math question: compare, do not calculate more than a simple difference.
